Mr. Speaker, I was just about to make that explanation when the hon. member rose. The bill, as hon. members learned when it was before this house, is largely technical in character. A very large number of the amendments were textual in that they substituted the word "army" for "military". When the bill came before the other place it was decided that it would be desirable, instead of making the proposed amendments to the various statutes by deleting one word and substituting another, to set out the section as amended in each case. That was done, and that disposes of all the amendments proposed by the other place with the exception of one.
There is only one amendment which is not of that character. I want to make it plain that all the amendments proposed in the other place, with one single exception, simply have the effect of replacing the whole section with a new section rather than merely substituting for the amended word the word of the amendment. Therefore they are not substantive in any respect whatever. The single exception is also purely of a technical nature. When clause 16 came from the other place it was found there was a clerical error in the amendment to clause 16 as it was proposed. This error would result in the reenactment of a provision of the Veterans Land Act in the same language in which it appeared prior to an amendment made in 1949. That amendment brought the definition of "veteran" in the Veterans Land Act into line with language used in the Pension Act. If we were to accept the proposed amendment to clause 16 in its present form, we would be restoring the law as it existed prior to the 1949 amendment, which of course would be undesirable. In other words, in proposing this series of amendments in the other place the law officers there in one instance used the name of a statute which is no longer its proper name, and I propose to move an amendment to this amendment in order to correct that error.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT TO PROVIDE FOR COMPENSATION, PENSIONS, ETC.   CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS   CONSEQUENTIAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the
consequential amendment proposed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is one that should be made, and I am glad to support it. But I feel that with respect to the series of amendments sent to this house by the other place I must say that I regard

them as the most ridiculous set of amendments I have seen in parliament for a long time. The Minister of National Defence has pointed out that, with the single exception of the case which he now seeks to correct, none of the amendments proposed by the other place has any effect in substance whatsoever. All that Their Honours have done is to make the Canadian Forces Act two or three times more bulky than it already was in the form in which it went through this house.
I have taken the trouble, because after all it is our job as members of parliament, to check the amendments proposed by the other place and to compare them with the sections in the House of Commons bill which they seek to amend. I find that out of twenty-nine sections in the bill Their Honours have rewritten in whole or in part twenty-two of them. I find, as the Minister of National Defence has pointed out, that in most cases they have rejected the House of Commons proposal for a simple amendment that just changes the word "military" to "army" or something like that. In its place they propose that the whole of the section be deleted and that the section as amended be put into the amending statute. I appreciate the fact that those who put forward this idea in the other place said that the purpose was to make the law more clear. I suggest that they have added to the confusion.
As the bill was brought into the house by the Minister of National Defence, drafted I take it by our law officers, I think it was not too bad. In each specific case where an act was being amended it was set out in the simplest possible language. For example in subsection 1 of section 3 of our bill we said that wherever the word "military" appeared it should be struck out and there should be substituted therefor the words "naval, army or air". I submit that when one is looking at a statute and learns that it is amended it is far easier to tell what the amendment is if the amending statute draws your attention to the one word that has been changed, pinpointing it as our bill did, rather than having to read the whole of the section over again as Their Honours propose and then go back and read it two or three more times to try to find out what the difference is in case it escaped you the first time you read it.
I submit that Their Honours have done a ridiculous job and have made the whole thing far more confusing. If that is the best they can do in the other place it is time the other place was abolished. Let me give some concrete examples. Section 3 of the bill as passed by this house consisted of seventeen

lines of type. By the way, it is 11 point type, 24 ems wide. Their Honours replaced it with a full page and a half of 9-| point type, 30 ems wide. There is no reason why I should not add to the confusion-since that is what Their Honours have done-by introducing these technical terms. But my point is that if we go through this bill section by section, and accept Their Honours' proposals that we delete a few lines and put in twice as many lines, or that we delete a few lines and put in two or three pages, the result will be that when we get through, instead of having a relatively simple bill such as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) brought in, we will have a very complex document.
I point out further that, in ordinary practice, people who have to refer to statutes do not for the most part refer to the original act and then to the amending statutes. What they normally refer to, in ordinary practice, is an office consolidation. That office consolidation is prepared in such a way that amendments such as these are incorporated in their proper place. I know office consolidations are not supposed to be admitted in court; but in ordinary practice they are used by those who wish to find out what the law is in a given case.
But in addition to the practice of using office consolidations, we have at this particular time in our legislative history the fact that we are revising the statutes of Canada. We passed an amending bill in respect to that only a few days ago. We know from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that when those revised statutes come out they will be known as the revised statutes of 1952, and they will include all the legislative acts passed by parliament up to the end of 1951. It seems to me quite clear from that that these minor technical, one-word changes made by the Minister of National Defence in his bill will be distributed through the various statutes, and this amending bill will no longer be one to which people will have any occasion to refer, at all.
It looks to me as though Their Honours realized they do not have anything to do. They just thought up a job for themselves and, instead of giving the country evidence that they are working, they simply have given the country evidence of the fact that that other institution should be abolished.
