Mr. Speaker, I think the policy of this house has usually been to accept tables for the record without reading them. I think it would be a mistake to depart from that policy and put on the rec ird reading matter that is not in the form of tables. I know that in the United States congress they put whole books on the record, and the first thing that will happen here, if we are not careful, is that we will be doing the same thing. If the names are not very long I suggest to the hon. member that he read them.

Well, I am quite willing to do that, but it will take ten minutes of the time of the house. I think it is of sufficient importance in the circumstances to justify putting it on the record. Suppose I leave this and put it on after I finish the rest of my remarks; then people will be able to find it. In case there is no time we shall leave it until probably the committee stage of the bill or until some other time. It may be that hon. members will not find it of sufficient value to take up our time with it; but certainly there are some impressive names and titles among the names listed in this group.
At that time I endeavoured to form a sound opinion, and I felt, after all the studying I was able to do, that probably the St. Lawrence seaway project was one for some remote future. At least I was not in favour of proceeding with it under the circumstances which then obtained in Canada.
I have endeavoured to keep more or less in touch with the whole project and the development of thought in respect of it. Everything that has come to my hand I have filed away and read as soon as I could find the time and the energy so to do.
An example of the documents I have considered is one called "The Great Lakes-St.

St. Lawrence Waterway Lawrence Seaway", which I am sure all hon. members have had, by J. G. McLean, vice president, apparently, of the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen, and national legislative representative in Canada. His article appears in the July, 1951 issue of The Brotherhood of Locomotive and Engine-men's magazine. I am not able to find exactly what is the standing of this gentleman, but anyway the document is here. I think it is worthy of respect. It seems to be written objectively, and the general feeling one gets is that the person knows a great deal of what he is talking about. I should like to read short excerpts from this document. On page 5 he discusses the No. 1 argument-that going forward with the project would provide for lower freight rates. He says: "Actually there is no assurance that it would." No. 2 is found on page 8. He says:
The second argument previously mentioned, i.e., the project would provide for additional sources of hydroelectric power, is the most poignant argument in favour of the proposed seaway.
Therefore he gives considerable respect to argument No. 2. On the same page the third argument is discussed. It reads:
The third argument concerning the encouragement of American capital investments is the most contentious of all.
By the way, these are not all the arguments the minister gave. The fourth argument, also found on the same page, is this:
The last argument, which supports the seaway development which suggests that the plan will strengthen the national defence, lacks any serious merit.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members, including the ministers, will not blame a person if, after reading such documents as this and every other kind that he can get his hands on, he finds many questions still unanswered. This was the reason I wanted to ask a number of questions. I will be given the opportunity of asking those questions when the bill is in committee stage, but I thought this array of evidence ought to remove from everybody's mind the thought that I was endeavouring to obstruct the other night when I desired to hold up the project long enough to ask some questions that were in my own mind.
As I said when I spoke first on the project, Social Crediters will favour it because I believe we all have a sort of feeling it is the right thing to do; that it is good for the country, and we are pleased also that Canada is going ahead with it regardless of United States assistance. That commends itself to us. I said all this, of course, when I first talked on the subject. At the same time I wanted to keep myself open-minded, ready for information on either side of the situation, in case we might have made a conclusion rather too hastily.

I will say that, with respect to all these documents' to which I have referred, the unanimous testimony of the witnesses was definitely against the immediate construction of the St. Lawrence seaway project in 1940. The one I read recently goes down to 1951.
I feel that the other night the minister made a magnificent speech. I do not know that I have ever heard a better one, better documented, better supported, better developed in every way and more beautifully expressed.
The question will be raised then: why are you not impressed by the statements from boards and other great authorities from whom the minister quoted? Well, I am going to tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to tell hon. members and the government why. Our age is an age of dangerous propaganda. The means of influencing public opinion today are so much more potent than anything heretofore known in the history of the world that we fail to appreciate what propaganda -can do. And the means of influencing public opinion are so completely available to men of wealth and influence and so unavailable to people without wealth and without influence that every man and woman in the nation and in this House of Commons has to exercise the greatest reservation before he takes for granted an idea which is disseminated, propagated, and stimulated by high-pressure propaganda. I am going to mention just two illustrations, and I hope I shall not be out of order in so doing, just to show how careful a person has to be.
Hon. members will recall the tremendous outburst of propaganda which filled our newspapers from coast to coast, and cluttered up our radios in every direction, all advocating the Sirois report in 1941. The actual facts were that the Sirois report was one of the most pernicious documents ever advocated by a body of men in the history of the Dominion of Canada. I am not going into detail on that matter but I shall challenge anybody to disprove what I say; yet Canadians were almost stampeded in respect to the stand on the Sirois report. You found great headlines, often in colours, in some of the newspapers. "The people of Canada demand adoption of the Sirois report," but not one per cent of them knew what it stood for. That was the kind of trash that was poured out all over the pages of our newspapers.
We have seen the same thing in respect to this St. Lawrence seaway project. There has been well-paid, carefully calculated and subtly executed propaganda to prepare the people for it. Probably nothing like that was meant, but every person who tries to

keep his feet on the ground and his head down out of the clouds has every reason to be reserved.
Here is another thing. Hon. members recall the Bretton Woods agreement. From the newspaper and radio propaganda that was carried on in support of the Bretton Woods agreement you would have thought it provided an entrance into kingdom come, that the minute we accepted Bretton Woods the whole lot of us would go right into paradise. All parties except the Social Crediters allowed themselves to be stampeded on Bretton Woods. When the thing was passed many members of the house thought, "well, we have done it; now our troubles are over." As a matter of fact that was the most dangerous thing Canada ever accepted in all her history, and was one of the major causes of the troubles under which the world is now struggling. But you could not even get a hearing when you attempted to reason about Bretton Woods. Hon. members in this house can remember that. So I take with reservation what almost anybody says. We are in an age when confusion is being sown deliberately by certain people.
There is another reason I have endeavoured to be cautious, as I am sure all people in Canada would expect me to be, or demand that I be, being in the opposition. The secret knowledge which may or may not have something to do with the desirability or undesirability of the construction of this project is not known to the people of Canada or to the members of parliament. There are no means whereby we can acquire that knowledge, no matter how diligent we may be in search of it.
The next difficulty is that we cannot tell whom to trust. I do not propose to give any illustrations of the way in which some of the most eminent men have allowed themselves to be tools in the hands of powerful interests in order that statements might be made which would advance the cause of those interests. I must say that I was under considerable anxiety and uncertainty when I was asking questions the other night. I was anxious, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) advises us to be, that there be adequate discussion of this matter before we put our signatures to so important a contract as one involving an agreement to build the St. Lawrence seaway.
Since I spoke last in this house I have had the opportunity of obtaining a copy of a speech delivered by General McNaughton. He is a man whom I trust to the highest degree. I am not unmindful of the fact that he is a great scientist, that he was a great general in the last war, that he is a man of
St. Lawrence Waterway courage and integrity. I am not unmindful of the fact that he occupies the important position of chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission and also chairman of the Canadian section of (the permanent joint board on defence. I think we must accept the word of such a man.
It would be contrary to all the principles of becoming deportment for him to let me know the inner facts upon which he based his conclusions. That is one of the unfortunate elements we must allow for. If he were to let me know, there would be no reason why he should not let others know. While I believe I could be completely trusted, I am afraid there are one or two that perhaps could not be. That means that I find myself without access to the fundamental facts upon which this man would base a statement similar to the one which he made in Toronto on December 6. May I read from the speech which that great man made; and I think we will all agree that we can call him a great man. Referring to the St. Lawrence seaway, he said:
-it has now become most urgent that an early start be made on construction.
This need for early action applies not only to the works contemplated on both sides in the international section of the river for power for which there have long been unsatisfied markets in each country for their respective shares; the need applies also for early action on the construction of the navigation facilities which recent estimates show will be used, well up to capacity, as soon as they are made available and because their absence has become a serious disadvantage to the trade and commerce of Canada.
Further on he used these words:
The representations which have been made to the congress of the United States favour the combined project for navigation and power as conferring the most far-reaching benefits to the peacetime economy of the two countries; they make clear also that the early completion of the works for navigation and power is a vital matter in relation to the defence of the North American continent in this period of deep anxiety and great concern.
In addition to the favourable report and recommendation given by the international joint commission, the project for the combined development of the St. Lawrence for navigation and power has been repeatedly before a succession of national advisory committees and the like both in Canada and the United States. In every case the project has been endorsed.
It has also received the attention of a series of joint engineering boards, where the design of the works required has been developed in great detail and to the point that there is no longer any significant question outstanding between the technical representatives of the two countries.
And further down:
The St. Lawrence project for navigation and power neither in its physical dimensions nor in its financial implications is that colossal, stupendous undertaking that some people have set out to picture, but I would agree that these superlatives will properly apply to the useful effects on our

St. Lawrence Waterway
economy and defence arrangements which will come from its construction, more particularly at this rime.
And the final quotation from that speech is is follows:
The board, after searching analysis, stated the project would increase military potential out of all proportion to expenditure in manpower and critical materials, much of which would be required to be used in any event as additional power had to be provided.
Having in mind these considerations and reaffirming its previous recommendations for the construction of the St. Lawrence project for navigation and power the board recommended:
"That the two governments take immediate action to implement the 1941 St. Lawrence agreement as a vital measure for their common defence."
Thus there is now on the public record the advice of the two bodies which have been created by Canada and the United States jointly to consider matters of mutual interest and concern along our boundary both for peace and for defence-the international joint commission, established under the waterways treaty of 1909 and the Canada-United States permanent joint board on defence, set up by President Roosevelt and Prime Minister King at Ogdensburg in August, 1940, have both recommended-repeatedly-that the St. Lawrence project for navigation and power should be built and promptly.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that such a pronouncement coming from this man at this time leaves me with no possible alternative but to support the measure without qualification.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks regarding the St. Lawrence seaway, I want to point out that for two reasons I do not wish to say anything with respect to the power phase of the project. One is of course that it is probably a very sound idea, and the second is that it is primarily a provincial affair. However, I should like to make a few remarks with respect to the navigation aspect of the St. Lawrence seaway development. I must say to begin with that I do not share the almost unbounded enthusiasm that certain hon. members seem to have for the scheme. We should remember that geographically our country is very large and spread out, that our population is very small, and that we already have a great and costly system of transportation which our economy must carry. The per capita cost for transportation is already very high, and we should be most careful indeed before we add to that load. We cannot but add to the load if we proceed with this very expensive development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
It may be of course that from a navigational point of view the St. Lawrence seaway would be such a stimulus that our economy would strengthen and our population grow to the extent that shortly the per capita load cost for transportation would be reduced. But I have seen no proof that that will be so, and I actually doubt very much if that will be the case. I have considerable doubt about the almost limitless enthusiasm of some hon. members that we can make ourselves rich merely by carrying products from one place to another and carrying other products back again. That type of economic philosophy reminds me somewhat of the gentleman in Georgia who had purchased a small truck, and who had $50 operating capital. With the $50 he bought a mule, and transported the mule across the county, after which he traded it for a cow. He transported the cow to another corner of the county and traded
St. Lawrence Waterway it for two sheep. He took the sheep to another part of the county and traded them for two goats; and he sold the goats to one of his neighbours for $50. His neighbour said, "You have been very busy, but where did it get you? You started out with $50 in the morning and this evening, after expending a great deal of energy, you have ended up with $50." The first gentleman replied, "Yes, I know, but look at all the business I did."
I am afraid that is the attitude some people are taking about this St. Lawrence seaway problem. We are not necessarily going to strengthen our economy by carrying goods from one place to another. What we should attempt to do is create sources of supply near the markets and create markets near the sources of supply. Let us so far as possible cut out all this business of having to carry goods from one end of the country to the other.
But, as I say, even if it can be proven that from the standpoint of transportation the St. Lawrence seaway is economically sound, there are many other side effects we should guard against. I cannot see where this is by any means an unadulterated benefit, an unmixed blessing. There are side effects which, if precautions are not taken, will have a very detrimental result upon the economy of certain parts of this country. An example of what I mean would be the development of our vast iron ore supplies in the Labrador area. Precautions should be taken to see that the economy of Canada is not reduced to that of a nation of primary producers and kept indefinitely on that basis, due to the fact that the iron and steel industry of the United States has the momentum of an earlier start and, for a time, can possibly carry on more cheaply than we can in Canada. We should see to it that, if necessary, an embargo is placed upon the export of iron ore needed for the production of goods we require in Canada, both for domestic use and for purposes of national defence. I can see no future for us, as Canadian people, in mining ore in Labrador and shipping it to the United States for smelting and rolling into sheets, then exporting it back to Ontario perhaps to be manufactured into automobiles, refrigerators and all that sort of thing, and finally to have it sold to the people of Labrador and the maritime provinces in a finished state. I see very little future in that.
We should make every attempt to develop our industries for ourselves. In that connection I am happy indeed to observe the broad-minded and statesmanlike attitude taken by certain members from the central provinces. But equally I deplore certain

St. Lawrence Waterway examples of provincial viewpoints, as they have been expressed in the debate. I resent the suggestion that if everything is well with the St. Lawrence valley, everything will be well with this great country of ours from coast to coast. That does not necessarily follow at all. That sort of narrow, provincial viewpoint is expressed by those people who at this late date, after almost a century, would revert to referring to this great country of ours as Canada. They would describe as Canada this dominion which stretches from sea to sea, "from the river unto the ends of the earth." They would describe it as it was originally described when it was two colonies in the St. Lawrence valley known as the Canadas. After all, in the beginning we were a group of colonies. We entered confederation so that we would no longer be separate and small colonies but rather we would be a great dominion, a great nation, a great domain from sea to sea. I am sure one of the reasons the fathers of confederation agreed to giving the name Canada to this new nation was that that name should be preceded by the word "dominion". The idea was that the Dominion of Canada should spread from coast to coast, from sea to sea and, to use the biblical reference, "from the river unto the ends of the earth".
If Canada is to become the great nation which is and should be its heritage, then it should be the concern of the government to try to look at our problems in a national way and consider all areas of the country. I do not think that as a nation we can prosper if there are depressed areas, if there are areas where there is not sufficient opportunity even to absorb the natural increase in population. I am shocked by the report in the last census which shows that the population of Saskatchewan has actually decreased in the last ten years. In this great country there should be all kinds of opportunities, not only for those who are bom here but also for those who immigrate to this country from the crowded areas in other countries.
The same is true of the maritime provinces. Ever since confederation the maritimes have been unable to absorb their natural increase in population. In that part of Canada there is not the opportunity there should be. Until we look upon our problems as those of a great area from the Atlantic to the Pacific, as problems that must be tackled for the benefit of all of us, I do not think we can hope to progress.
Therefore I support this scheme for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway only if it is a part of a greater scheme, only if it is one little bit in a large and beautiful mosaic of development which will make this country of ours the great nation it has the


right to be. So I suggest that we embark as one great nation upon a purposeful, energetic and broad-minded program for the development of the whole of this great country from sea to sea, and "from the river unto the ends of the earth".

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned at 6.15 I was just beginning to deal with the subject of iron ore and the argument made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and some other hon. members, that we should look twice before exporting our iron ore. That statement and others that are allied to it deserve some consideration, and I propose to deal with it as best I can at this time. First of all I should like to say that the government yields to no one in its concern that Canadian resources should be developed to their maximum, and that Canadians should get the greatest possible benefits in employment and other forms out of these developments of our natural resources.
Our concern is as active in the case of the Quebec-Labrador ore deposits as in the case of any other resource. We certainly do hope to develop markets for iron and steel. Our hopes do not stop there, either. We will do all we can to develop markets for Canadian products made out of that iron and steel. At the same time, however, it is clear that in Quebec and Labrador we have iron ore in such quantities as to be surplus to any such domestic requirements for many generations to come. We do have markets that can be opened up for that ore. Steel mills that are now in existence are looking for new ore supplies, not hypothetical mills that are to be built at some vague time in the future.
Without relaxing our efforts to create a larger steel industry in Canada, based on

export markets, we wish at the same time to open up other markets that I have just mentioned for our iron ore.
I think the case of the Quebec-Labrador deposits can be compared with that of the Wabana iron ore from Bell island of Newfoundland. The Bell island deposits, as the committee knows, are made up of one of the largest deposits of hematite known in the world. Hematite is an ore with a comparatively high iron content. The Bell island mines are the main source of ore for the Sydney steel mills. But a large part of the production of Wabana ore is exported, and has been exported for many decades. Large new export demands have initiated an expansion program now under way that will mean a great increase in production. Anyone so irresponsible as to oppose this development would be attacked and with good reason, I am sure, by the very people who are complaining now that the iron ore from the Quebec-Labrador fields should not be exported. Why? Because the potential production of Wabana ore far exceeds any likely requirements of the Sydney steel mills for many generations to come.
Then if one looks again at the deposits at the Steep Rock and Michipicoten mines in Ontario the position is the same. Both ores are used to some extent in Canadian blast furnaces, but large quantities of lower grade ore are imported to mix with them in the furnace charge, while a large volume of the Canadian ores is shipped to the United States. Why? Because it is more economical to "sweeten" the low-grade with the high-grade in the furnace charge, and the high-grade ore is more valuable for this purpose than for direct charge to the furnaces in Canada.
Quebec-Labrador ores are high-grade too. However great the volume of steel production that may be achieved in Canada, it will always be to our advantage to exchange a quantity of high-grade ore for lower grade imports.
I think the same can be said of wheat. We have large quantities of wheat in this country, and we export large quantities; but we also mill large quantities. Other countries have flour mills, too, however. We are able to export our flour in competition with other countries. While our mills are competitive in cost and do get a large share of the world's milling business, they do not get enough of the world's milling business to keep them going. That is why it is necessary to export wheat. We do all we can to develop our flour markets, but I do not think any hon. member would suggest that we stop at that
St. Lawrence Waterway and refuse to export any of the wheat that is surplus to the requirements of the Canadian flour mills.
The same thing applies to the base metals, copper, nickel, lead, zinc and such other metals. A high proportion of the ores are smelted and the metal refined in Canada. In most cases there is a considerable domestic fabrication of the metal as well, and in some cases we do a sizeable business in the processed product, as for example, copper wire and cable.
I think, in so far as Quebec-Labrador ore is concerned, our objective is the same, but on the face of it the basic factors are not the same. Our success with base metals stems directly from the importance of cheap hydroelectric power in the reduction process. We do not have a comparable advantage in the case of iron and steel. The position does hold some promise, but I would be misleading the house if I were to say without equivocation that we can have the same success with iron and steel that we have had with base metals or for that matter with paper and other products that have been mentioned. But I do say that we will bend every effort to get the maximum advantage for Canada out of our iron ore resources.

Marie is spending $40 million to add 360,000 tons to its pig iron capacity,

Is not the answer to the fears expressed by the coal miners in Nova Scotia the fact that the greatest opposition in congress against the building of this canal was from the United Mine Workers of America?

I have just one word to say about the cost and then I shall resume my seat. The information we have is that it will certainly not cost that much. In so far as the power aspect is concerned, that is to be looked after by the province in conjunction with an appropriate authority on the United States side of the line, so this house is not called upon to consider any expenditure in so far as that angle is concerned. Neither is the house called upon to consider any expenditure so far as the navigation portion of the project is concerned. It is estimated that the navigation feature of the project will cost $245,993,000, which is broken down as follows: In the Lachine section for navigation alone, $98,229,000; in the Soulanges section, $37,116,000; in the lake St. Francis section, $2,513,000; in the international section, $106,833,000, and in the Welland ship canal $1,302,000, making a total of $245,993,000.
It is expected that these sums of money will be liquidated by the imposition of tolls. Surveys have been made in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it is anticipated that by the imposition of tolls throughout the seaway it will be possible to liquidate the scheme over a period not exceeding fifty 94699-114

There is nothing so extraordinary about that, That has been considered by both the government of the United States and the government of Canada, and we are of the opinion that the scheme can be liquidated by the imposition of tolls in the manner set out in the bill. I think perhaps I have said enough at this stage. As I said earlier, I think we have been fortunate in that most members have found it possible to support these projects. If that is so, I am hopeful that from this point we shall be able to proceed more effectively than heretofore.

My anxiety, as the minister is aware, for an early start on this undertaking prompts the question I now want to put to him. I imagine it is a question that is in the minds of a good many members who are desirous of seeing the plans proceeded with. As I understand it, Canada must,go to the United States government for, certain consents before the plan can go forward. When Canada goes to the United States for these concessions or consents, as the case may be, to develop the international rapids, can congress, if it follows its procedure in the past, block that, or has the United States government full power to give such consents?

I do not think I should
attempt to answer any questions as to what any foreign power can do. I will be glad to assist the house as to what is my understanding of the procedure. We have, I think, full authority to build the canal on our side. The province of Ontario will require some cooperation with an appropriate authority on the other side of the line, but if I were to attempt to answer questions as to what is likely to happen in congress I might well make a misstatement which I would regret afterward, and I would rather not. On the subject of asking questions, we are on section 1, and my understanding is that when we deal with the sections seriatim we can probably have the questions then. St. Lawrence Waterway suggesting that it might take place on the other section. However, I am in the hands of the committee.

When the minister was dealing with the steel companies of Canada he mentioned Dosco in Cape Breton. I would have liked him to go a little further and say that the plant there was to be greatly enlarged. After hearing the minister speak about these plants, one is inclined to ask why there is a scarcity of steel in Canada. When I spoke in the interests of the maritime provinces the other day with respect to the seaway project, I supported the idea that something definite should be promised us, and not only my own province. Indirectly we would derive great benefit if the steel plant at Sydney were one of the big steel plants of Canada.

Substantial expansion is taking place at the Dominion Steel and Coal Company at Sydney. As I indicated, it is an expansion which will amount to $44 million, the first phase of which is $16 million. My hon. friend says there is a scarcity of steel but it is not only in Canada. There is a scarcity of steel all over the world. It is one of the most critical materials.

The other night I asked the minister the following question, as found at page 1689 of Hansard for December 7:
Has the government any plans for a great expansion of Canadian steel production?
The whole tenor of my remarks was based on that question. I take it from what the minister has said tonight that there is to be no greatly expanded steel production plan for Canada arising out of these huge deposits of iron ore in northern Quebec and Labrador. He has explained that there is some expansion going on in the present steel plants, but apparently there is no broad scheme based on these huge resources. Can the minister tell us what percentage of the ore from northern Quebec and Labrador is to go to the United States? The department must have made some estimate of the amounts that will be used in Canada and the amounts that will be going to the United States. If the minister will recall, I quoted the other day a portion of the evidence given by Mr. George M. Humphrey, president of the M. A. Hanna Company of Cleveland, before the House of Representatives public works committee in Washington. In that statement he said that from 2 to 4 million tons of iron ore a year would be going to the United States Atlantic seaboard for use in the steel mills there, and that 6 to 8 million tons would be going up the St. Lawrence for use in United States steel mills in the lake Erie district.


These figures add up to a total of 10 million tons, which I understand is the estimated annual production from the new ore body. What is the expected proportion that will be used in Canada and what proportion will be going to the United States?

I do not think anybody can answer the first part of the hon. member's question. The railway is not completed yet. The ore has not moved from Burnt Creek and Knob Lake to Seven Islands. It is not expected it will be moved before 1954. So until that time arrives it will be impossible to answer the hon. member's question.
The statement which Mr. Humphrey made I suppose deals with this position: when they do move their ore to that port of Seven Islands the St. Lawrence seaway will not have been completed. They have to get their ore out of there. They have to get it down to the market. So they will get it, I presume, down to the Atlantic seaboard ports. They will also move it to ports on the St. Lawrence, so I am informed, and from there move it by rail to the great lakes area. They will do that until such time as the seaway is completed, when they will be able to move it in the specialized carriers I mentioned earlier.

The point I made was that, according to Mr. Humphrey, all of this iron ore is to go to the United States. Surely the government has made some investigation into the possibilities of using some of this iron ore in Canada. From what the minister said a moment ago he would not be able to answer that question until the railroad is completed and the first train of iron ore gets down to Seven Islands. That surely is ridiculous. The government surely must have given some thought to what proportion of this ore is to be used in Canada, and what proportion is to go to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I can throw some light on it. I think my hon. friend has a misconception of the relationship of the ore business to the steel business. For example, we will take the Algoma Steel Company, which uses roughly 1,200,000 tons of ore a year. At the mine some fifty or sixty miles away they produce about that much ore-that is, about 1,200,000 tons a year. Of that ore Algoma itself uses about 300,000 tons. You say: "Why is that? That does not seem reasonable".
They mix it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
A steel company must have many kinds of iron ore for the kind of products they are turning out at the time. You have two or three types of ore for an open hearth charge, and a different type

of ore for a Bessemer. It is common to put all this ore into what we call the great lakes pool of ore and to draw from that pool such ore as is required; also to put into the pool such ore as is surplus to the requirements of the owners of the pool.
It would be very difficult indeed to know definitely what was going to happen to Steep Rock ore next year. As a matter of fact the bulk of Steep Rock ore goes to the United States, for the reason that it is a very high grade of ore and no Canadian furnace can afford to use too much of it. AH Canadian operations, I think, use some Steep Rock ore.
Then, getting back to the St. Lawrence, the stock of the Iron Ore Company I believe is owned by six steel companies, and by Hollinger and by the Hanna Company. I understand that there are eight owners. Mr. Humphrey as quoted was speaking about certain ore which has been allocated to certain steel companies. I understand each of the steel companies has contracted for a certain amount of ore. I understand those contracts represent about 50 per cent of the output of the mine. The railroad and dock facilities are being geared for an output of 20,000,000 tons of ore a year. So about half of it is sold on firm contracts, and half of it will be offered on the markets of the world.
It is anticipated that the Canadian mills will take such proportion of the ore as they can use. I have no doubt that Dosco will take a portion of their ore from this source. I am sure the steel mills on the great lakes will use a portion of that ore. But I do not think any man can say three years ahead where all the ore will be marketed. I certainly could not. It is anticipated there will be a good market in Europe. I understand there is a firm market for about half the output in the mills represented by the ownership of the property.
My hon. friend asked if the government has a plan. The government does not build steel mills; it never has, and probably never will.
They help.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We help, of course. And I might say that four years ago I was so sure we needed additional capacity that I had put in the speech from the throne a proposal to help finance the expansion of the steel industry to about the size that is being built at the present time. I was not able to convince the mills that such capacity was needed. I regretted it very much. The best I could do was not good enough, and the capacity was not built at that time. Had it been built then Canada would have been in a much more comfortable position during the last two or three years, the last two years at least.
94699-114i
St. Lawrence Waterway
However, we do try as a government to keep the economy in reasonable balance; and we always try to see that the basic ingredients of industry are provided in ample supply. We stimulate that sort of development. That is why we are financing the mechanization of coal mines in Nova Scotia at the present time. That is why we have done everything possible to facilitate the expansion of steel mills. I might point out to my hon. friend that today Canada is not self-sufficient in steel, or I should say in ore. We use more ore than is mined in Canada at the present time, even though we export ore from Newfoundland, for the reason that its geography is such that it cannot be used in Canada. It is too far away.
They are exporting ore from British Columbia, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend thinks that is unfortunate. I am not so sure. I am just as anxious to develop Canada as he is. I hope he will give me credit for that. I will give him credit for being as anxious as I am. But it seems to me that the opening up of that ore is the first important step toward a steel industry on the west coast. Steel industries have been interested in that situation. They are faced not only with building a steel plant but with opening up a great ore-mining industry, which is expensive indeed. At least in future they will have three mines open on the island. That may give a selection of ore, or it may give all one grade of ore; I am not sure. But I would hope that out of the three widely separated points there might be a selection of ore. The fact that they can see that ore, the fact that shipping facilities are there, and the fact that it is being mined is a great inducement toward building a blast furnace to use that ore. Probably half the capital expenditure is already made when those three deposits are being mined.
I believe you have to do first things first. I believe you must first be sure of your raw product before you can go on to the later stages of development. That has been true of almost anything Canada has done. We first mined copper and sold most of it as ore. We have now built a great fabricating industry in the field of copper, and we export more finished products of copper than the refined copper. That is true of zinc, and it is true of lead. The proportion of zinc fabricated in Canada as compared with zinc produced in Canada goes up rapidly every year.
By first opening up the iron ore-and by "opening up" I include the improvement of the St. Lawrence because that certainly opens up that ore to the steel mills of the great lakes-I believe that is the first

St. Lawrence Waterway Important contribution to the expansion of steel that will follow, as it always has followed in this country. Our steel capacity has been expanding steadily for a good many years.
We are still only producing about two-thirds of our requirements, are we not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We were producing before the war. about three million tons and importing about one million tons.

Is there not apt to be a tremendous increase in the demand for steel? Take for example the oil pipe lines, and developments like the aluminum plant in central British Columbia, and the development at Lynn Lake, as well as various other developments in Canada on a scale greater than we have ever had. Is it not likely there will be a tremendous increase in the demand for steel within Canada? If that is so, should not some more aggressive steps be taken to increase our steel capacity? The minister had admitted that a year or two ago we really needed the expansion of our steel industry, but it did not take place because the companies were unwilling to go ahead. We do not want to get into that position again. It does seem to me that the demand for steel is going to increase at a greater rate in the future than it has for years past.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As an optimist, that is my own view. My hon. friend and I are optimists. You could have a basic steel expansion for the isolated projects the hon. member mentions, projects that will be finished in the next two or three years. I am sure we both believe there will be other projects to follow for which we shall need more steel.
Such as the South Saskatchewan and St. Lawrence waterways projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, they will take some steel. Nevertheless, there is an expansion of 33 per cent in capacity in progress at the moment. Blast furnaces are being built and finishing capacity is being installed. In order to justify a steel plant you must have three things. You must have iron ore available; you must have coal available, and there are several other ingredients you must have available which are less important. But above all you must have customers within reach. This accounts, of course, for the location of the steel plants we have. The owner of a steel plant always keeps his eye on the customer situation to make sure the plant can operate at an economic level, and that is usually about 60 per cent of capacity.

Is there any reason steel plants could not be successfully installed on the lower St. Lawrence?
[Mr. Howe.l

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You would have the iron ore there, but you would be still a long way from the coal and you would be an even longer distance from customers. I believe the latter ingredient would be most difficult. You would be moving finished steel instead of the ingredients.

Will the minister indicate when this steel expansion program about which he talks will have shown results? A few days ago I believe he said that it would be perhaps 1953 before we began to see the results of this 33 per cent expansion in basic steel. Will he indicate what part of that 33 per cent is being made at the Sydney plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The first results of the expansion are already operative. The blast furnace which was built within the last 18 months at the plant of Dominion Foundries and Steel in Hamilton is now in operation, and we are getting the benefit of that additional production. The expansion at Sydney is in the direction of finishing capacity, because at Sydney the production of primary steel was out of balance with finishing capacity. As the hon. member knows, we were shipping billets from Sydney to be finished in Montreal and Hamilton. Additional finishing capacity is being put in so the operation will be brought into better balance. Just when it will come into production, I cannot say. I understand that $14 million is being spent in the present operation as part of a $40 million project. I am not familiar with the details.

I have always been under the impression that when the St. Lawrence project was completed ocean-going vessels would travel up to the head of the lakes to pick up cargoes of grain. In his speech the other day the minister made it clear that this will not be the case. It will only be the case where a vessel has an inbound cargo. Otherwise the cargoes of grain will continue to be brought to Montreal ;by lake steamer and transferred at Montreal to ocean vessels. At page 1579 of Hansard for December 4, 1951, the minister said:
The prairies would find a substantial saying in the cost of moving grain, flour and other products to markets in eastern Canada and overseas.
If the grain is going to continue to be brought down by lake steamer and then transferred at Montreal to the ocean-going vessels, where is the saving in cost?

The savings will be in the
disappearance of the 14-foot canals. Today grain is taken from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne, Prescott and such places

179X
as Port McNicoll. There it is transferred into smaller ships and brought down to Montreal.

In the
course of the debate the other evening I made a reference to a statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. May I recall what I said, as it appears on page 1695 of Hansard for December 7:
I hope I do not do him an injustice when I say that the hon. member for Cape Breton South seemed to me to favour nationalization, that the government should take over the business if private enterprise is not willing to do it.
Here is what the hon. member said as it appears at page 1674 of Hansard for December 6:
As I suggested when I spoke before, I am prepared to support this project as one part of a large public investment program by the federal government. This authority to be set up should have the right to develop any potential power or other resource within a reasonable distance of that area.
Then in the next paragraph but one he said:
I think the government would be well advised to have another basic steel plant. This would not be asking very much.
Further on he says:
A new plant could be set up or the Sydney plant could be expanded, possibly by the use of public funds.
Well, if I misinterpreted the hon. member's remarks I am very sorry, but it seemed to me to be plain, from those and other remarks he made with reference to what is going on in Newfoundland at the present time, that he seemed to favour a policy of nationalization of the steel industry. The hon. member went on to make reference to Newfoundland. I can forgive him for what he said about me, but he made some remarks about Newfoundland which I believe he would not make again if he had the opportunity. On page 1697 of Hansard for December 7 he said:
. . . after years and years of the kind of development visualized by my hon. friend, Newfoundland stood as a rather badly undeveloped and in every way neglected section of North America. In 1944 I heard a representative of the British government make a report to a meeting in London.
On the next page, he said:
After listening to the report of that commission of government on the educational standards, the economic backwardness, the lack of sanitation and everything that was not modern in this world, if I had not known the section of Canada that was being referred to I would have thought the representative of the British government was describing a section of South Africa where civilization has just gone in to make a survey.
Now, sir, I have here a document published by the Department of External Affairs and entitled "Newfoundland, Canada's New Province". This document contains a statement of the expenditure per capita on education in the year 1944 in Newfoundland,
St. Lawrence Waterway the year to which the hon. member referred. Apart from what is spent by religious institutions and contributed by charitable bodies, Newfoundland spent $9.35 per capita; Prince Edward Island, $7.74; Nova Scotia, $9.41 and New Brunswick, $8.80. Therefore educational standards in Newfoundland stand up very well in comparison. Apart from that, sir, Newfoundland had the distinction even in this country of having higher educational standards than most of the provinces. I do not know to what the hon. member was referring as economic backwardness, because in 1944 Newfoundland had its highest foreign trade on record; it was over $100 million. He speaks of the lack of sanitation. Is a country going to be judged by the system of plumbing which it has? If -that is so Italy and France as well as many other European and South American countries would come in for general condemnation, as would pants of this country.
Newfoundland came in for condemnation for having everything that was not modern in this world. Down there we have the largest pulp and paper plant in the world, and we have the best fish-processing plant in the world. But apart from that-, I think everyone who has been to Newfoundland will recognize the fact that we have a law-abiding and Christian people, even if we have not all the modern facilities we might have. Those who go there enjoy themselves. Thousands of Canadians and Americans who went there during the war spoke very highly of Newfoundland. Only yesterday I heard a gentleman high in the civil service of this country state that the week end he spent down there was the happiest in his life.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that we are getting away from the matter of the seaway.
Mr. Chairman, I only wanted to draw to the attention of the committee the incorrect statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of tying up the committee. What the hon. member for St. John's West thinks-
Speak louder, please. What you are saying is of the utmost interest.

Whatever the hon. member for St. John's West thinks or says in this chamber is not a great national issue. I have no intention of tying the committee up on the matter. What I objected to a few nights ago was the hon. member's misinterpretation of what I said. He has clearly indicated now that he does not know the difference between the nationalization of an industry, what I propose to the government, and what is going on in

St. Lawrence Waterway Newfoundland. Nationalization, as I understand it, means that there is an industry set up and the government decides to take it over. They are nationalizing an asset that was created by someone else, and it is generally done on the basis of compensation; but it is the taking over of an established industry. What I proposed to the minister, and it is relevant to the bill before the committee, is that this now is a government development. The taxpayers are going to provide the capital. I suggested that what should be done, if possible, was to do it in a manner similar to the T.V.A. development in the United States in so far as we can do it. That was a government-sponsored project. It was on a co-operative basis. There is not anything that would suggest its nationalization. It is operating now successfully in the United States, and I think it is an outstanding example of what can be done by government research, competent engineering, capital and direction by the government. There is no suggestion of nationalization there.
The same thing is true in Newfoundland. The government of Newfoundland is providing the capital, or at least 50 per cent of it. It is giving this encouragement to industries to come in. The Newfoundland government is creating something. They are not taking something over. It certainly is not nationalization. The expansion of the steel industry talked about by the Minister of Defence Production is being done along exactly the same lines. I think I am safe in saying that 50 per cent of the capital that is going into our present steel expansion is government money given to the industry to encourage them to expand in a time of crisis and need. That certainly is not nationalization. Perhaps the hon. member caught me in a rather unhappy mood the other night. When I said what I did, I did not mean anything disparaging.
Now you are sorry.

No, I am not sorry. I am never sorry for anything I say; but I am in a better frame of mind tonight, and perhaps I am more reasonable. I did not have any intention of being disparaging or of casting any reflection on Newfoundland. The hon. member for Melfort, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar and myself heard Lord Ammon make a report of a survey on social and economic conditions, with particular reference to the outports in Newfoundland; and the description that I and the other members along with me heard left a great deal to be desired along many lines. But of course there are many sections of Canada to which the same description might be applied. I


do not want to tie the committee up any longer. I am quite satisfied with what I put on the record, if the hon. member for St. John's West is now satisfied. It is not a great national issue, as I said before.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

May I thank the hon. member for Cape Breton South for his explanation. I just want to point out one thing to him, namely that there is a difference between what is going on in Newfoundland and what he said, because the Newfoundland government is actually setting up in that province industries financed with government funds and operated by the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister one question. If he has dealt with it he can tell me so readily. I appreciate the position he took with regard to any questions as to the position taken in the United States. If my question transgresses the position he took, of course he can tell me and all is well; but I should like to put this question to him. Is there any point-and I mean point in time-beyond which it would no longer be possible for the undertaking to be a joint Canada-United States undertaking?

I think I can answer that question. Yes, there must be a time. When that time is I am unable to say, other than to repeat the general statement made by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada to the effect that if congress did not come along at an early date, then the President of the United States would be quite prepared to approve of this project as a second best choice, on condition that we would undertake to build the seaway.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister says that he is not able to indicate the exact date, although he realizes there has to be a point. Does the bill now before us close the door in any way or set any time beyond which there could not be a joint undertaking?
No, it does not.
Is there any relation between the works that will be done for the hydroelectric project and the works that will have to be done for the seaway project?
No, there is not.

Last year some time a committee of the congress of the United States came here to talk the matter over with a similar committee in Canada, of which I think the Minister of Transport was chairman or with which he was connected is some official capacity. I have often wondered about it. There was a great deal of talk at that time

about this committee of the congress of the United States, and that they were here to discuss this St. Lawrence deep waterway. What was their reaction when they bade good-bye to Canada and had nothing more to do with this St. Lawrence waterway? Did they consider it to be an impossibility, or why did nothing further develop from that meeting of the committee of congress with a similar committee in Canada?

The committee that came to Canada to view the site of the Long Sault rapids was a committee on public works of the House of Representatives of the United States. It is not the first time similar committees of both the House of Representatives and the Senate have come to view the sites. They did not come here to deliberate with any opposite group in this country. They simply came to take a look at the works and to see the situation for themselves. That was only part of the visit which began at the Mesabi range at the head of the lakes, went right down through the whole of the project along the United States side and into the Canadian side at Beauharnois and Lachine, and ended at Montreal.
I was in contact with the chairman of the committee, Mr. Buckley. During his stay in Canada, he was sanguine about the whole thing. But of course he had to go back to the public works committee of the House of Representatives, which he did. I understand that some discussion took place later there, and that the bill which was under discussion at that time was not reported to the floor of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I do wish to refer back to comments that were made by the Minister of Transport before the dinner recess. At that time he seemed to express some measure of surprise that so much time had been devoted to the discussion of iron ore, when we were in fact discussing a deep waterway project. But the fact is that the discussion of iron ore was introduced by his own statement to the house at the time he was explaining the advantages of this development. And one of the things which it would seem not only points up this discussion on the basis of the use of iron ore but also raises some additional measure of concern on the part of representatives from the maritime provinces was the emphasis which he placed upon the fact that this seaway would make it possible to convey the iron ore to great steel mills in the United States. I refer to what is reported at page 1576 of Hansard, where he had this to say:
Now it also promises to be the key that will unlock for the future the iron ore fields of Quebec and Labrador. It will open large new markets for these ores in the great lakes area, otherwise largely
St. Lawrence Waterway
out of economic reach. And on the other side of the coin it will give those interior steel mills the best new source of ore at the lowest cost, a matter of serious concern at the moment.
Iron ore. The mills within reach of the great lakes account for about 75 or 80 per cent of the steel produced in United States. They draw ore preponderantly from the iron, ranges of the lake Superior district. The immediate problem is not the exhaustion of these ores, although that too may be expected at some more or less indefinite time. The point is that production of the ores now in use has just about reached its maximum annual rate, and that maintenance of even that rate promises to involve a continued increase in costs. Meanwhile ore requirements continue to rise, not only because of additions to steel capacity but because with a shortage of scrap it is taking more pig iron to make a ton of steel. The problem thus is one of a growing gap between supplies and requirements.
The minister went on to explain, that the construction of this deep waterway would make it possible for the iron ores from Quebec and Labrador to sell at prices which would make it possible for that iron ore to be sold to those great mills in the United States. May I emphasize the fact that in no remarks I made at any earlier stage did I suggest that we should not export iron ore to the United States; and so far as I am aware that argument has not been made. The argument that has been made is that there should be assurances that we are going to make the maximum possible use of iron ore in this country.
There are reasons why it would not be proper for us to place an absolute prohibition on the export of iron ore. Very large sums of money have been invested by companies in the United States in the development of this iron ore. It is unlikely that the maximum production now under way would have been actually yet undertaken were it not for the fact that companies in the United States had been prepared to invest capital in this venture. I do not think Canadians will wish to have the contracts of those companies disregarded at any time, or to see any suggestion of repudiation of the basis upon which we have encouraged and accepted investment in this country.
Having said that, however, we then come to what is to be done to encourage a greater use of iron ore in this country. We have heard speeches by hon. members from the maritime provinces which indicate very clearly the great concern they feel about the emphasis that is being placed upon the facilities that will be offered for concentrating still further industrial production in the central part of this country. I for one do not believe that anything except our own lack of vision could possibly prevent immense increases in industrial development in the central part of the country. I share, however, the sentiments of the hon. members from the maritime provinces, and I have already



St. Lawrence Waterway expressed my belief that at a time when the government is undertaking to spend so much of the people's money to provide facilities of this kind, it should give clear and positive evidence that it is going to take whatever effective steps it can to assure that there will be as great a decentralization of industry in this country as possible; and that local demands are created for iron ore in these areas where there will be opportunities not only to produce iron and steel for the local and Canadian markets, but also to export from seaboard to the markets of the world finished products from the iron and steel which could be made there if the steps are taken to provide power at low cost that could be taken, and which have been discussed here oh other occasions.
I would recall the remarks of the Minister of Transport when he took up the suggestion he understood had been made by one hon. member that probably this iron ore would be largely carried by ships from the United States. He pointed out that there is a very large program of shipbuilding now under way in Canada, and that just within these past few weeks some of the largest freighters ever built in this country, or in fact on this continent, have been launched, the last of them just within the last two or three days. I think there is evidence, as he says, of the confidence that is in the minds of many Canadians, and may I add also of people living in the United States, that there is going to be a great expansion of shipping, and that accounts for the number of these new ships that are being built. However, time will tell whether the preponderant part of that ore will be carried by Canadian ships or by ships from the United States.
I wish to deal particularly with what the minister said about the production of iron ore at Steep Rock and also of aluminum in processed form at Arvida. He asked: what has happened at Steep Rock? What has happened at Arvida? What has happened to the development of pulp and paper? He asked these questions in relation to the use of ships, and indicated that Canadian ships were carrying large quantities of iron ore from Steep Rock and aluminum from Arvida and pulp and paper from the great mills along the waterways of the interior of Canada. I think the question he asked, though, produces an answer that does underlie the importance of some further efforts being made to assure Canadian use of the iron ore. What has happened at Steep Rock is that that rich concentration of iron ore is going to the United States, whether in Canadian bottoms or in bottoms from the United States. That is not a limitless source of ore; that is something that cannot be replaced when it is

gone. It is true that a good mine has been developed there and that money is coming in for that ore, but we are receiving that money at the lowest level at which ore can be sold, except that ore which, as has already been mentioned, is being used in mills in Canada in mixture with other ore.
There is a difference between shipping pulp and paper and shipping iron ore. Pulp and paper is the result of a crop. True it is not an annual crop, but it is a recurring crop over a long period of years. It is a crop that can be maintained indefinitely if proper methods are employed. That is not true of iron ore. We are exporting pulp and paper because steps were taken to make sure that the highest possible employment would be created through the actual processing and manufacturing of wood products in this country. No objection was taken in the United States when the provinces of this country showed adequate concern over their legitimate self-interest and introduced a manufacturing clause into the contracts under which pulp logs were cut. If there are any people in the world who recognize legitimate self-interest it is the people of the United States, who have always practised that principle in relation to the development of their own resources.
In his earlier remarks the minister said this was something that the provincial governments could do, that it was not something the dominion government could deal with. The provincial governments have no authority over export as such. The provincial governments exercise control over export by licensing the cutting and making contracts under which the raw materials are used. The control they exercise over export is not direct, but there is effective control exercised by the terms they impose in the contracts under which the right to cut is given.
The dominion government has the right to deal with export and to impose any terms on export that it sees fit. As many hon. members will recall, we discussed for some considerable time certain questions relating to the export of oil and natural gas. It was fully recognized at that time that the dominion government and the parliament of Canada have the responsibility of dealing with export of that kind. There is no question about the fact that the dominion government and the parliament of Canada, where it is necessary to pass laws to deal with the subject, have authority. In fact they have the only authority to deal with exports as exports. I point that out because hon. members from the maritime provinces and from other parts of Canada which are not going to benefit

directly in a way that can be seen at the moment, or to the extent of the central provinces, wish to have some indication that the government is prepared to use the authority it possesses, either under legislation now in existence or by legislation to be introduced, to assure the maritime provinces that where it is within their power they will take proper steps to bring about a greater decentralization of industry and an expansion of industry in the maritime provinces. That can be done so long as iron ore to be produced in this way is available under favourable terms to mills in the maritime provinces which could smelt it and produce pig iron or steel to be used ultimately in the industrial activities that could be encouraged in that way.
As has been pointed out, it is true that the dominion government does not build mills or directly actually enter into industrial developments of this kind in the ordinary course of events. However, the fact remains that the dominion government is exercising substantial influence on the location of plants by the fact that it is taking steps to assure certain types of production, and in taking those steps of course it has a great measure of choice as to where the developments will take place.
I recognize that this is not something that can be dealt with overnight. These are longterm plans that are being discussed. It is going to take considerable time for the railroad into the Quebec-Labrador ore areas to be completed and for the actual production of ore to reach the point where it will be flowing out to the port from which it will be carried. However, that very fact gives us time to take those steps which would encourage the increased construction of milling capacity in different parts of Canada to use the ore when it becomes available. In fact, if the plans are made now and encouragement given at this time, the mills would hardly be more than ready when the ore would actually be available for their expanded capacity.
It has been explained to us tonight that at Sydney, Hamilton, the Sault and elsewhere construction is under way. It has also been explained that the dominion government has actually assisted in the financing of the mechanization of the operation at Sydney. But it seems to me we should bear in mind that we have a statement by the Minister of Transport that we now have reserves of iron ore on such a scale that within no measurable term of years can we expect to seriously deplete the total reserve. We also have something else. We now have a mixture 94699-115
St. Lawrence Waterway of different types of ores to an extent which we did not have only a comparatively few years ago.	.
Therefore it would seem only reasonable for us to examine just what our target should be, recognizing that most of us in this house believe in the free enterprise system and the development of operations of this kind by proper investment under proper encouragement. What is the target we should be aiming at? It has been mentioned that with a demand of something in excess of four million tons we have been producing a little over three million tons. But every hon. member knows that we are very short of iron and steel at this time. Every hon. member knows also that we are importing large quantities of products of all kinds made from steel which might well be made here if sufficient encouragement were given. Therefore we cannot measure our needs simply by what we are using at the present time. If we were producing the same amount of steel in this country that is produced in the United States in proportion to population we would be producing approximately thirteen million tons instead of just over three million tons. It has been explained that work is under way which will substantially increase our steel production, but only by a small fraction of that requirement based on our use of steel in the same proportion that it is being used in the United States. I think our target is a point far beyond that. We are seeing this country develop as it has never developed before; but we are only seeing the beginning of what can come in a country that now has such vast quantities of iron ore, oil, uranium and the other things which will go into industrial expansion in the years ahead.
Our target should be something like 15 million tons of steel a year, and even that will be far below what this country will be requiring within a comparatively few years. It will be far short of the amount the country can use to great advantage if we recognize that steel is the metal base of industrial development and economic strength. As I mentioned in an earlier speech, for centuries alchemists tried to transmute base metals to gold. Today we do not need to transmute iron to gold; it is the most precious metal of all. We have iron ore, we have electric power and we have oil available in ever-increasing quantities. We have inland waterways to carry the ore and our finished products back and forth. We have harbours at the seaboard to ship our finished products to the markets of the world. It is one of the most challenging prospects that has unfolded before any nation.
With all that has happened, we are now entering the period of greatest opportunity

St. Lawrence Waterway this country has ever seen, and that opportunity will be largely measured by the encouragement that is given to processing, finishing and manufacturing based on steel. I am not talking only of processing to the point of the steel ingot. I am talking of all the associated industries that will grow upon the expanded use of steel in Canada. Just as Great Britain suddenly emerged from the stage just over a hundred years ago where its population was a little more than our population today to a position of great international power and wealth, this country is at the beginning of a historic period when we may see our population grow to numbers far beyond anything we have yet dreamed.
When I say that I am not suggesting, as is said -sometimes, that we should suddenly start shuttling ships across the ocean bringing large numbers of people here. If we hold in this country the population that is born and brought up here we will be increasing our population a great deal more than it has been increased for some time. Population also has a habit of adjusting itself to the capacity of a country to support population. In the United States the population has grown because of the employment created through resources which they have put to such good use. That is what we should be looking forward to in this country, and what we can look to with great advantage at this time.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has spoken of the fact that from the economic point of view we must export ore for the purpose of opening up this development. Very well; let that be done. But let us remember it is Canadian ore that has been found in our own soil and, while we encourage others to come here and make developments of this kind, when we spend huge sums of money to make it possible to move the ore back and forth we can also say very appropriately that Canadian consumers should have certain advantages in the use of ore that we produce in our country. There is nothing unreasonable in that attitude. There would be nothing unfair to the people of the United States or elsewhere if by appropriate measures we actually create more favourable terms for the Canadian industrial consumer of our ore so we might encourage great industrial development based on this raw material in the same way that we encouraged industrial development in the use of wood products a few years ago and made it the greatest money earning industry we have in the country today.
While this discussion takes place on the first section of the bill in committee after it has received second reading, I should like to point out that what was under consideration on second reading was the principle, and I think
