it is greatly to the credit of hon. members, who come from parts of the country that feel their position may be jeopardized by a measure of this kind unless certain assurances are given to them, that they should have accepted the principle contained in the bill and not voted against it, although there may be so many reasons from their point of view why it is difficult to make a decision of that kind without much stronger assurances than they have been given in the bill now before us.
Now we have the details presented to us for consideration. I hope the Minister of Transport will reassure those members who have expressed that measure of concern, and all of us who hope to see immensely expanded industrial production based on the use of iron and steel in this country, that along with a development of this kind, which according to the words of the minister will carry ore into that area where 75 or 80 per cent of the great steel mills of the United States now operate, steps will be taken to decentralize industry across Canada in every way possible. I hope he will reassure us that appropriate steps will be taken to give to the Canadian producer certain advantages in the use of our own ore which under a system of free enterprise and private investment will expand the steel industry and related industries of this country on the scale that is justified by the resources we now possess.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes to say a few words on the bill. Several members from the maritime provinces have expressed their views, and I should like to mention particularly the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, who spoke today. I wish to go on record as supporting to a great extent everything they have said. I realize that every citizen of the maritime provinces is very much interested in expanding our steel industry or any other industries that we may have, and in the creation of any new industries that might be set up there. I have spoken on the St. Lawrence waterway on two other occasions and expressed my views very clearly. However, there is one thing I have not heard discussed so far in this debate, and that is the change in the bill before us now having in mind suggestions that have been made in the years gone by.
I refer to the original agreement between Canada and the United States on the great lakes-St. Lawrence navigation and power project. When that was discussed originally many years ago it called for the free passage of vessels throughout the entire length of

the St. Lawrence waterway. At the present time such a policy exists on the St. Lawrence waterway. Vessels from all parts of the world use the canals and the waterway free of tolls. Under the proposed all-Canadian St. Lawrence seaway authority, tariffs of tolls will be established. At this point I should like to quote the Minister of Transport as he is reported at page 1707 of Hansard for December 7. The hon. member for Lethbridge had asked a question, to which the minister replied:
The United States have manifested great concern over it.
He was referring to the statement concerning the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway.
The position of the President of the United States is indicative of that, when he states that he is willing, if the congress does not act within a reasonable time, to consent to the development of this project in conjunction with us, both as to power and navigation.
In so far as the first part of my hon. friend's question is concerned, if he will only wait until the bill comes before the house he will find the seaway project is self-liquidating. He is going on the assumption that the taxpayer is going to be faced with a tremendous expenditure. In the original statement I made I indicated that it is intended to liquidate the whole project by the imposition of tolls.
If as the minister states this project will be self-liquidating-and I have no reason to doubt that statement-then there is little argument so far as the taxpayers of this country are concerned as to other parts of Canada which would not be benefited by the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway being obliged to pay their proportionate part of the costs.
That particular section in the bill will take away much of the feeling that has been created in the maritime provinces to the effect that we were paying a proportionate share of the cost of something from which we would receive no benefit. If the tolls which will be charged when the St. Lawrence waterway is completed will completely maintain operation and pay for the cost of building the waterway development, then there is very little in the way of increased taxation that can be used as an argument against this huge development, which I believe we are all pretty well convinced will be a benefit to all Canada.
When I spoke on this same subject on one or two former occasions I opposed it, stating that it was a project which, although financed by all the Canadian people, would bring no benefits whatever to the maritime provinces. But since I am convinced it will be self-liquidating, and that in the final analysis it will not cost the Canadian people anything, I cannot do other than support it.

Mention has been made of certain projects we would like to see developed in the maritime provinces. I believe the minister is well aware of them. In fact I have no doubt all cabinet ministers are aware of them. They have been brought to their attention on many occasions. I have faith in the cabinet and in the government, and I am going to support the bill without hesitation, convinced in my own mind that we in the maritimes will not be forgotten and that the many things we have brought to the attention of the government, which we feel would be beneficial to the maritimes if developed, will meet with the government's approval. I believe we can rest assured of their assistance.

Like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I have spoken on this project on other occasions. I wish now to make only a few remarks with reference to statements made by the minister before six o'clock. He indicated that because about $92 million was being expended in the maritime provinces we should not complain about the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. He made special reference to the Canso causeway in Nova Scotia. When I spoke before I made reference to that project. It is in Nova Scotia. I said that while those of us in New Brunswick will receive no benefit from the causeway at Canso, still we were anxious that the development should take place.
He mentioned also the ferry between Bar Harbour and Yarmouth in Nova Scotia. This, also, will be of no particular benefit to New Brunswick, but we have no objection to it. As a matter of fact it will be to the disadvantage of New Brunswick. It is for the development of the tourist trade of Nova Scotia. Whereas in past years cars coming from the United States came through St. Stephen and up through Saint John and Moncton to Nova Scotia, we will now lose that traffic on account of the ferry. He also mentioned the Saint John airport. Let me remind him that Saint John waited a long time for the airport. I doubt if there is another city in Canada that has waited as long or as patiently as the city of Saint John. It was entitled to the airport. Although we are always grateful for anything given to us, I do not think we need feel too grateful in this respect.
He made further reference to Fredericton, another city which waited a long time for an airport. He mentioned the ferry between Cape Breton and Newfoundland. He must know that the ferry between Cape Breton and Newfoundland was promised to the people of Newfoundland when they entered confederation. While we are grateful for these things they are what we should expect, what we are entitled to expect. The expenditures

St. Lawrence Waterway
on these developments are no greater than the expenditures on similar developments in all the other provinces of the dominion.
Airfields, causeways and ferries are good in themselves; but they do not make employment for our people. We would rather see the development of some project like the Chig-necto canal, or the project at Passamaquoddy, where cheap power would be produced in the maritime provinces and industry would be encouraged. That is what we ask for; that is what we feel we are entitled to, in addition to these other things the minister has mentioned.
My leader spoke about our fear of centralization of industry. That is exactly what we fear. We have seen our young people leave our province because of the lack of industry. We believe the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and St. Lawrence power will create more industry in the central provinces, and will take more of our young people away from the maritime provinces unless there is a power development in that part of the country.
I have very little more to say. The minister tried to leave the impression that because we had received $92 million for the development of certain public works we should be satisfied. We are not satisfied. We want developments which will increase industry and give employment to our people. That is what we are asking for, something along the lines mentioned by my leader tonight, and to which reference has been made on other occasions. I do hope the minister and the government will keep these things in mind. The hon. member for Charlotte has just said that the cabinet is well aware of the requests of our province for the development of Passamaquoddy and Chignecto. I hope they will keep those matters in mind. If the government helps in the development of these projects, then in time I am sure they will be self-liquidating and self-supporting. I am also satisfied they will bring industry to the maritime provinces. As no doubt the St. Lawrence seaway and power project will be a great blessing to the central provinces, so the development of these projects would be a great blessing to the maritime provinces. We would have in Canada not only a prosperous central section, but prosperity in the maritimes and other sections.
That is what we are asking for. We ask not only for a causeway, not only for the airports to which we are entitled anyway, but something further which will develop our industries.

Just before this section carries, may I say that I was not in the house the latter part of the afternoon when the minister


opened the debate, as I was attending the public accounts committee. I am not in a position, therefore, to discuss with him the proposed expenditures which I understand he enumerated. The hon. member for Royal has spoken about these moneys having been expended. I believe he is a little optimistic in that statement, judging from the projects I heard mentioned. They are still promissory notes, and are a long way from being cash. The causeway has been promised for at least twenty years, and bobs up before every election. Then, it subsides again beneath the waters of Canso strait. This time we are accepting the assurance that the government will go ahead with the scheme. Similar remarks could be made about the other projects mentioned.
I rise simply for the purpose of asking the minister if he would clarify one point he mentioned this afternoon. Specific mention was made of the proposed ferry from Bar Harbour to Yarmouth as something which has been constructed or which would be constructed. I might also let the minister know of a personal note in connection with that particular ferry. It has been promised for some considerable time. Plans were prepared and, as all hon. members know, this ferry means a great deal to the province of Nova Scotia because it does assist in the development of the tourist industry. I was shocked one day to read in the Ottawa Journal or the Globe and Mail a statement by the Minister of Transport that the construction of that ferry would be postponed because of a shortage of steel. I have not looked at my files to check the dates, but I believe that was about two years ago.
Then as I recall it, speaking again from memory and without trying to be accurate as to dates but it seemed to me within a week or two weeks, the hon. member for Stormont, who happens to be the Minister of Transport, speaking in his own constituency said the time had come when the St. Lawrence project must be proceeded with at once. If the government of the United States was not going to do it, then certainly the government of Canada must do it. To say the least, I was irritated and I believe many others in the maritimes were, at the suggestion, I know unintentional, that it was possible to find steel for such a huge project which meant much to the productivity of Ontario, but it was impossible to find a quantity of steel for a project which to some extent was comparable in that it would bring new dollars into Nova Scotia. I simply say that in passing. It still rankles when I hear this project mentioned. Since the minister has introduced the subject, and since there is some doubt as to when that ferry is to be built and when it is to go

into operation, I trust that when the minister closes this debate he will give us some information on these expenditures which I understand total some $93 million.

There is one matter I should like to mention to the minister, and that concerns the possibility of using the waterway for twelve months in the year. A huge amount of money is being spent to construct this waterway, and if some means could be found for keeping it open for twelve months instead of seven the value to Canada would be greatly increased. I am wondering whether the minister's department is doing any research into that problem, and is that possibility being kept in mind in planning for the waterway?
I was surprised to find in the Engineering Journal for June of this year an article entitled "The St. Lawrence Waterway, an AllCanadian and Very Deep Route." It is written by J. G. G. Kerry, M.E.I.C. who I understand is an outstanding engineer. As I read the article it suggests there is a possibility of keeping the waterway clear of ice.
That would be the last straw.

This possibility arises from the fact that lake Ontario never freezes. The suggestion is that if the free water could be channelled from lake Ontario into the river it might be possible to keep the waterway open all winter. For example, this author has this to say:
Such a supply of heat energy as is stored in. the waters of lake Ontario during the winter months is almost unique. It is a great national asset that the engineers of Canada should not fail to use to the greater advantage of Canada.
Such a plan may or may not be sound, but it does seem to me that the objective is of such great value that the department would be wise not to ignore any suggestion of that type, and not to construct the waterway in such a way that it would be impossible to adopt some of these schemes. A year or two ago when we were interested in atomic energy, I understood that eventually that power might be used for dispensing with ice. I suppose it is many years in the future, but could the minister tell us whether his department has in mind the possibility of some such scheme that would eliminate ice in -this waterway during the winter months?

The answer to that question is no. We in the department have no means or scheme whereby we can do away with ice. I am aware of the article to which my hon. friend refers, and so are the engineers in the department, but we know of no method whereby navigation can be kept open for twelve months in the year. We
St. Lawrence Waterway in the department know of no method whereby navigation can be kept open for a greater length of time than it is kept open. On the contrary, we are proceeding on the basis that it can be kept open for seven *or eight months only, because we are continuing our program of icebreakers. I am not an engineer, and I am not in a position to depreciate or appreciate the article to which my hon. friend has referred. All I can say is that we in the Department of Transport know of no method whereby the St. Lawrence can be kept open for twelve months in the year.

There is provision for adding to the authority additional canals and operations in the upper lakes, if that were required. It is not envisaged at the moment. That is all I meant to say. This clause is extremely
important; it has to do with the purposes, capacities and powers of the authority. I think the clause restricts any development except in the area set out in the clause, namely between Montreal and lake Erie.


That makes the thing pretty much a central Canada development. When I was discussing this matter I had hoped that the authority would be broad enough to develop in any part of Canada any power or similar project that might be in the interests of Canada as a whole. This does not give the organization, when it is set up, any wide authority but restricts its activities to the area set out in this particular clause. I suggest to the minister that there are other developments which might be undertaken.
This bill has to do not only with the development of that waterway. It gives the authority the power to acquire lands for constructing, maintaining and operating all such works, and so on. What I had hoped- and I still hope the minister will think about it-is that once this authority is set up, it is going to develop in Canada power projects and industries, if necessary, in certain parts of the country. I should like to see this authority broad enough to give them power to look at, for example, the 'Quoddy project in New Brunswick. It is just as necessary to the province of New Brunswick, to the states of Maine and New Hampshire, and to that surrounding area as is this power project to the province of Ontario and the state of New York. It would not necessarily mean that we would have to go ahead and develop it overnight. But as we are embarking on a program of this kind, I think my suggestion might be adopted. It is government incentive in opening up and developing the country where there are potentialities and where risk capital cannot be found. I think that is in accordance with the government's program announced in 1945. It now looks to me as though the government were starting to implement it. Why should we restrict the development to the area to which it is restricted under this clause?
If the minister added just a couple of words I think it would be quite satisfactory to everyone. I suggest that it would be satisfactory if something were added to the effect that this authority had power to develop projects between the port of Montreal and lake Erie, and in any other area where a project might be in the best interests of Canada. I think those words would broaden the effect of the section, and would give them the right at least to continue the survey that is being made of the 'Quoddy project and the Saint John river project. As we are now setting up this kind of machinery, I think it should be broad enough to include the whole of Canada, where the authority may determine that a project is necessary and desirable and risk capital cannot be found for it, such as your power in Ontario and in the state of

New York. I do not think that is asking too much. I do not anticipate that it will be done overnight but at least it would give to the bill and to the authority the proper designation, that given it by the minister, namely that this is in the interests of Canada as a whole. While he said that, this clause restricts the authority you are setting up to the short section between Montreal and lake Erie. Will the minister consider adding the provision that, as to any other project that comes within the scope of this authority and that might be in the interests of Canada as a whole, they could take a look at it, at least?

Much as I should like to accede to the request of my hon. friend who is so co-operative, generally speaking, and who is being co-operative at this time, I have to say that this is a specific project. That is why the government felt that the authority should be set up in the form of a crown company, along the lines of a former crown company, to deal with two things, namely the construction of the waterway and the operation of the works. If there were to be an extension, where would you draw the line? I think I know what my hon. friend has in mind. He is thinking of something along the line of the T.V.A. in the United States. The government, unfortunately for him in this case, has decided that it should be a crown company in this sense; and I have no authority to amend the bill as he has suggested, nor could I do so at this juncture.

Likewise it might authorize the seaway authority to take over other canals that are now operated by the Department of Transport, if it should be deemed necessary to do so.

Section agreed to.
On section 15-Tariffs of tolls.

As this takes in the Welland canal as well I gather that it will be possible, under this authority, to charge tolls on the Welland canal?
St. Lawrence Waterway
Yes.
As I read it, section 15 would empower the authority to charge tolls on the Welland canal, would it not?

Yes, but on the Welland canal only in so far as the cost is concerned. I indicated a moment ago that it would cost about $1,200,000. I have forgotten the figure I put on the record. Only as to that expenditure and the cost of the operation of the Welland canal is it the intention to charge tolls. I put on the record how the cost of amortization would be disposed of; and in so far as Welland is concerned, it would only be for the expenditure at Welland.
Power contained in the section is broad enough to enable the levying of a regular toll in the Welland canal?
Oh, yes.
Does that conflict with any existing arrangements we have with the United States in regard to the use of that and other waterways?
No, it does not.

It seems to me the government is determined to have this put through. They have had excellent cooperation. I do not think we have ever experienced such co-operation in this chamber before, but I might say a minimum of consideration. It is after ten o'clock, and I think we have done enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

No.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will take up the following items: The debate on the address; Bill No. 33, to establish the St. Lawrence seaway authority; Bill No. 34, respecting construction of works for the generation of electric power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river; then the three resolutions: one, to amend the Dominion Elections Act; two, the resolution respecting the national gallery and three, to amend the Civil Service Act. Then, if we have time, we shall take up Bill No. 17 to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, and Bill No. 8, to amend the North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act.
At 10.05 o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on November 2, 1951.
